06:30 PM\n\t\t\t\t\t101 button Watch\n\t\t\t\t\t102 text Level 3\n\t\t\t\t\t103 text Level 4\n\t\t\t\t\t104 text Level 5\n\t\t\t\t\t105 heading Synopsis, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t106 text Synopsis\n\t\t\t\t\t107 text Luckily for LSAT students (who tend to hate math), there isn\'t much math in LR or RC, but once in a while we are tested on some pretty math-y stuff.\n\t\t\t\t\t108 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t109 text Mainly this will happen in  Must Be True  and  Most Supported . But sometimes we resolve a math-y  Paradox , and sometimes we prove a math-y conclusion in  Sufficient Assumption .\n\t\t\t\t\t110 text Collectively, this accounts for about 4% of questions, so we normally only see 1 question per LR section pushing us into the math zone. \n\t\t\t\t\t111 button Read More\n\t\t\t\t\t112 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t113 heading Common Concerns, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t114 text Common Concerns\n\t\t\t\t\t\t115 text The biggest chunk of Math-y Stuff is probably occupied by \n\t\t\t\t\t\t116 text Quantifiers\n\t\t\t\t\t\t117 text  like "some / most / all / few". There are "Venn Diagram" overlap inferences we can make by combining certain claims.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t118 text Quantifier Inferences\n\t\t\t\t\t\t119 text GIVEN:\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Most A\'s are B\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Most A\'s are B + Most A\'s are C + Most B\'s are ~A INFER:\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0 Some B\'s are C\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0There are more B\'s than A\'s\n\t\t\t\t\t\t120 text GIVEN:\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Most A\'s are B\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0 Most A\'s are B + All B\'s are C  +\xa0\xa0All A\'s are C INFER:\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0 Most A\'s are C\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0 Some B\'s are C\n\t\t\t\t\t\t121 text GIVEN:\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0 All A\'s are B\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0 All A\'s are B + Some A\'s are C + All A\'s are C INFER:\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Some B\'s are C\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Some B\'s areC\n\t\t\t\t\t\t122 text Percent vs. Number\n\t\t\t\t\t\t123 text The percentage of females at a certain company can increase by adding females to the company or by subtracting men (or both).\n\t\t\t\t\t\t124 text LSAT authors always forget about this 2nd way. They think that any percent increase in X is caused by an increase in the \n\t\t\t\t\t\t125 text raw number\n\t\t\t\t\t\t126 text  of X. But it\'s possible that it\'s caused by a decrease in the number of \n\t\t\t\t\t\t127 text not-X. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t128 text If we have a 10 person company, 6 women and 4 men, then the company is 60% female, 40% male.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t129 text If 2 men join we\'ll have a 12 person company, with 6 women and 6 men. Then the company will be 50% female, 50% male.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t130 text Notice that the company just went from being 60% female to being 50% female. An LSAT author would erroneously assume that this means that females left the company, but no females left. We have the same 6 women as we started with.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t131 text The percent of the company that is female is calculated by taking the fraction of females out of the total.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t132 text \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Was\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0 Now FEMALES \xa0\xa06\xa0\xa0 \xa0\xa06\xa0\xa0 \xa0\xa0 TOTAL\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa010\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0 12\n\t\t\t\t\t\t133 text % female\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa060%\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0 50%\n\t\t\t\t\t\t134 text LSAT authors always think that a percent is changing because the numerator is changing, and we need to understand that it can also change from the denominator changing.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t135 text Similarly, if we hear that the rate of car thefts is down (10 years ago, 15% of people had their car stolen but now only 12% of people had their car stolen), that doesn\'t mean that the \n\t\t\t\t\t\t136 text number \n\t\t\t\t\t\t137 text stolen cars is down.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t138 text This city might have had a population of 1 million ten years ago but now has a population of 2 million.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t139 text 15% of 1 million people\xa0\xa0<\xa0\xa012% of 2 million people\n\t\t\t\t\t\t140 text So the number of stolen cars is higher now, even though the rate / proportion / percentage of people who have had their car stolen is lower. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t141 text Gambler\'s Fallacy / Being Too Literal \n\t\t\t\t\t\t142 text Sometimes LSAT authors will think, "If the last three flips of the coin have been tails, then the \n\t\t\t\t\t\t143 text next \n\t\t\t\t\t\t144 text flip is more likely to be heads", but that is not true. Each flip is an independent even with a 50% probability of heads or tails.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t145 text Sometimes LSAT authors will think, "The average income in this neighborhood is $100k per household. Betty lives in this neighborhood, so her household must bring in $100k." That is interpreting average too literally. Betty\'s house might make way above or way below the average.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t146 text They might interpret a ratio too literally and say, "The ratio of boys to girls in this class is 5 to 7. Since three girls just left the class, the ratio must now be 5 to 4." It\'s possible the class started off with 20 boys and 28 girls, which is a 5 to 7 ratio. If three girls leave, then now it\'s 20 boys and 25 girls, which is a 4 to 5 ratio. Ratios are relative ideas, not real numbers. We\'re not allowed to take a real number like "3 girls left" and apply it directly to the ratio.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t147 text Weighted Average\n\t\t\t\t\t\t148 text When two things are mixed together, we get something in between. When we mix black coffee with white milk, we get some form of brown or tan, depending on how much of each we use.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t149 text A drop or two of white milk in black coffee will make it a dark brown.  A drop or two of black coffee in white milk will make it more of an eggshell white.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t150 text Similarly, we can do this with statistics. If the average age of Company A is 40 yrs old and the average age of Company B is 30 yrs old, then when the companies merge into one, the average age of the employees will be somewhere between 30 and 40. If the average age of the new company is 35, then we\'ll know that an equal number of employees from Company A and Company B were involved (just like if we combined 1/2 coffee and 1/2 milk, we would get a shade of light brown that\'s halfway in between white and black). \n\t\t\t\t\t\t151 text If the resulting age is more like 33, which is closer to Company B\'s average age, then we\'ll know that more of the employees of this new company came from B than from A. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t152 text If the resulting age were something like 39, we\'d think, "Wow this new company is almost entirely people from Company A, with just a few youngsters from Company B sprinkled in."\n\t\t\t\t153 image Quantifiers\n\t\t\t\t154 text Quantifiers\n\t\t\t\t155 text Not Started\n\t\t\t\t156 button Start\n\t\t\t\t157 container\n\t\t\t\t\t158 text Video\n\t\t\t\t\t159 button Watch\n\t\t\t\t\t160 text Level 2\n\t\t\t\t\t161 button Start\n\t\t\t\t\t162 text Level 3\n\t\t\t\t\t163 text Class\n\t\t\t\t\t164 text Thu, Aug 27, 08:30 PM\n\t\t\t\t\t165 button Watch\n\t\t\t\t\t166 text Level 4\n\t\t\t\t\t167 text Level 5\n\t\t\t\t\t168 heading Synopsis, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t169 text Synopsis\n\t\t\t\t\t170 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t171 text The topic of Quantifiers relates to questions in which LSAC is testing our ability to manage statements with words like  some / many / most / few / all / not all . They are testing our ability to see when certain traits must overlap or don\'t have to overlap.\n\t\t\t\t\t172 text For the most part, this is only relevant to Must Be True questions, Parallel and Parallel Flaw questions, and a few Sufficient Assumption questions.\n\t\t\t\t\t173 text Overall, it only accounts for 3% of LR questions, so on most tests we have 0 or 1 question testing quantifiers. Because of that rarity, be careful about getting too worried by or sucked into this topic. It tends to be a weird one that students find perplexing and might obsess over, which isn\'t the best use of study time. \n\t\t\t\t\t174 button Read More\n\t\t\t\t\t175 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t176 heading Approach, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t177 text Approach\n\t\t\t\t\t\t178 text Some people like to diagram quantified statements. They would look at a claim like, "Most clowns are scary" and write it down like this:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t179 text Clown --m--> Scary\n\t\t\t\t\t\t180 text The \'m\' in the arrow is reminding us that this isn\'t a conditional logic arrow, which implies certainty. It\'s a most-arrow, which only implies something is probable. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t181 text If I tell you that Bob is a clown, you can use this rule to tell you that "Bob is probably scary". Just like conditional logic rules, you cannot reverse these or negate these.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t182 text We can\'t say,  "Bob isn\'t a clown. Thus, he\'s probably not scary." (negation)\n\t\t\t\t\t\t183 text We can\'t say,  "Bob is scary. Thus, he\'s probably a clown."(reversal)\n\t\t\t\t\t\t184 text Diagrammers would look at the claim "Some cowboys are poets" and write it down like this:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t185 text Cowboy <--s--> Poet\n\t\t\t\t\t\t186 text The double-sided arrow is communicating that this statement \n\t\t\t\t\t\t187 text is \n\t\t\t\t\t\t188 text reversible. It\'s true to say "Some cowboys are poets" and it\'s true to say "Some poets are cowboys". \n\t\t\t\t\t\t189 text Other people (like Patrick), find it crazy to diagram quantified claims, both because it\'s unnecessary and because it confuses our brain when it comes to how we usually use arrows to represent certain/universal conditional logic. So experiment with diagramming vs. not-diagramming to see what works.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t190 heading Quantifier Inferences, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t191 text Quantifier Inferences\n\t\t\t\t\t\t192 text For the most part, quantifier inferences are just applying a conditional logic rule to a fact, but there are two exceptions, which involve \n\t\t\t\t\t\t193 text two Most claims\n\t\t\t\t\t\t194 text .\n\t\t\t\t\t\t195 text The most common Most+Most inference we make is a \n\t\t\t\t\t\t196 text Trait Overlap \n\t\t\t\t\t\t197 text inference when we have two Most claims about the same group.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t198 text For example, if we know ... \xa0\xa0Most clowns are scary \xa0\xa0Most clowns are trained actors\n\t\t\t\t\t\t199 text Then we can infer there\'s a trait overlap between "scary" and "trained actors". There has to be at least one person (whom we happen to know, in this case, is a clown) that is both scary and a trained actor. So we can infer "some scary people are trained actors" as well as "some trained actors are scary", which are of course the same statement (since Some statements are reversible). \n\t\t\t\t\t\t200 text The math-y form of this looks like this\n\t\t\t\t\t\t201 text GIVEN:\xa0\xa0Most A\'s are B \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Most A\'s are C INFER:\xa0\xa0\n\t\t\t\t\t\t202 text Some B\'s are C\xa0\xa0(Some C\'s are B)\n\t\t\t\t\t\t203 text A more rare form of Most/Most looks like this ...\n\t\t\t\t\t\t204 text GIVEN:\xa0\xa0Most A\'s are B \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Most B\'s are not-A\n\t\t\t\t\t\t205 text That allows us to infer that there are more B\'s than A\'s. For example, "Most Senators are men. But most men are not senators". That tells us that there are more men than Senators.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t206 text Everything else in Quantifier Town is really just applying a conditional logic rule to a specific fact. The other inferences we make are based off \n\t\t\t\t\t\t207 text All / No \n\t\t\t\t\t\t208 text statements, which are condionals.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t209 text GIVEN:\xa0\xa0All clowns are scary. \xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0\xa0Some clowns are poets. INFER:\xa0\xa0 \n\t\t\t\t\t\t210 text Some poets are scary\xa0\xa0(some scary things are poets)\n\t\t\t\t\t\t211 text When we see "all clowns are scary", we can think\n\t\t\t\t\t\t212 text clown --> scary\n\t\t\t\t\t\t213 text Anywhere that we see the word "clown" we can add the idea of "scary", so when we\'re told "Some clowns are poets", we know that those poets are also scary, since \'clown\' automatically conveys \'scary\'. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t214 heading Resources, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t215 text Resources\n\t\t\t\t\t\t216 text Here\'s Laura\'s quantifier \n\t\t\t\t\t\t217 link Description: sheet, Value: docs.google.com/presentation/u/0/d/1opeTzppatuGlZbClZ4-m54OAbAXFUqqA9dKNM9XRUx0/edit?usp=sharing&pli=1\n\t\t\t\t\t\t218 text . And here\'s \n\t\t\t\t\t\t219 link Description: Matt\'s, Value: assets.lsatlab.com/uploads/2022/05/Quantifiers_Diagram.pdf\n\t\t\t\t\t\t220 text . \n\t\t\t\t\t\t221 text Why doesn\'t Patrick have one?\xa0\xa0\n\t\t\t\t\t\t222 text Because he hates diagramming quantifiers. \n\t\t\t\t\t\t223 text :)\n\t\t\t\t224 image Assumption / Objection Family\n\t\t\t\t225 text Assumption / Objection Family\n\t\t\t\t226 text Not Started\n\t\t\t\t227 button Start\n\t\t\t\t228 container\n\t\t\t\t\t229 text Video\n\t\t\t\t\t230 button Watch\n\t\t\t\t\t231 text Level 1\n\t\t\t\t\t232 button Start\n\t\t\t\t\t233 text Level 2\n\t\t\t\t\t234 text Class\n\t\t\t\t\t235 text Sun, Sep 27, 06:30 PM\n\t\t\t\t\t236 button Join\n\t\t\t\t\t237 text Level 3\n\t\t\t\t\t238 text Level 4\n\t\t\t\t\t239 text Level 5\n\t\t\t\t\t240 heading Synopsis, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t241 text Synopsis\n\t\t\t\t\t242 text This topic doesn\'t come with a video lesson. It\'s meant for students late in their prep to toss all the question types from the Assumption / Objection family into a blender:\xa0\xa0Flaw, Strengthen, Weaken, Necessary Assumption, Sufficient Assumption, Principle-Strengthen, and Evaluate.\n\t\t\t\t\t243 text These questions collectively account for more than 1/2 of each LR section. They all involve evaluating an argument for assumptions the author is making or potential objections that we could make.\n\t\t\t\t\t244 button Read More\n\t\t\t\t\t245 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t246 heading Common Concerns, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t247 text Common Concerns\n\t\t\t\t\t\t248 text The Assumption family is the group of question types that present arguments and ask us to evaluate missing links or facts with the internal logic, or to consider possible overlooked considerations beyond what was brought up in the argument.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t249 text Question types like Sufficient Assumption, Necessary Assumption, and Principle-Strengthen/Conform are usually fixated on the internal logic of an argument (term shifts, conditional logic, triggers, outcomes, missing links, missing facts). In other words, the Conditional Logic reasoning structure dominates most of these.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t250 text Question types like Strengthen, Weaken, and Evaluate are usually more focused on potentially dubious Comparisons and speculative Causal explanations. We typically want to bring in \n\t\t\t\t\t\t251 text other \n\t\t\t\t\t\t252 text considerations, \n\t\t\t\t\t\t253 text new \n\t\t\t\t\t\t254 text ideas that might suggest a salient difference between two things or might suggest an alternate explanation for a curious fact.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t255 text Flaw is a weird hybrid, in which many answers call out assumptions and many answers bring up overlooked considerations. But in addition to that, Flaw also tests us on just recognizing certain Illegal Moves (such as all the famous flaws). Parallel Flaw mainly tests famous flaws or bad idea math.\n\t\t\t\t\t\t256 heading Skills to Build, Value: 2\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t257 text Skills to Build\n\t\t\t\t\t\t258 text As you work your way through Assumption Family question types, practice switching your mindset:\n\t\t\t\t\t\t259 content list\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t260 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t261 text • "In the box" thinking (the internal logic analysis of Assumption and Principle) \n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t262 container\n\t\t\t\t\t\t\t\t263 text • \ufeff"Out of the box" thinking (the new, overlooked considerations of Strengthen / Weaken / Evaluate). \n\t\t\t\t\t\t264 text When you\'re doing Flaw, open up your mind to considering famous flaws as well.\n\t\t\t\t265 link Description: Full Study Plan, Value: app.lsatlab.com/my/study-plan.php\n\t\t\t29 heading AI Skills Training Center, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t30 text AI Skills Training Center\n\t\t\t31 link Description: Start AI skills training center, Value: app.lsatlab.com/skills-training/\n\t\t32 container\n\t\t\t33 container\n\t\t\t\t34 heading Drill Engine, Value: 3\n\t\t\t\t\t35 text Drill Engine\n\t\t\t\t36 button Select Logical Reasoning\n\t\t\t\t37 button Select Reading Comprehension\n\t\t\t\t38 tab group Drilling mode\n\t\t\t\t\t39 tab (selected, settable, boolean) Adaptive, Value: 1\n\t\t\t\t\t40 tab (selectable, settable, boolean) Filtered, Value: 0\n\t\t\t\t\t41 tab (selectable, settable, boolean) Top Priorities, Value: 0\n\t\t\t\t42 text Adaptive drilling uses your analytics to pick which questions you see and at what level.\n\t\t\t\t43 button A, F1997, 1 - Bank and database keys agree for all 20. PT102-S3-Q14 has existing breakdown steps, so this draft supplies only its five missing notes. All other slots supply breakdown and five notes. No answer-choice disagreement identified in this subset. Model references are from the database; weaknesses noted in `models/Flaw.md` were not copied.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 1. PT101-S3-Q2 · Flaw · Difficulty 1 · Answer E\\r\\n\\r\\n*Modelled on PT150-S2-Q4 (comparison), PT107-S4-Q18 (test the abstract wording), and PT154-S2-Q12 (missing alternative).*\\r\\n\\r\\n> Advertisement: Anyone who thinks moisturizers are not important for beautiful skin should consider what happens to the earth, the skin of the world, in times of drought. Without regular infusions of moisture the ground becomes lined and cracked and its lush loveliness fades away. Thus your skin, too, should be protected from the ravages caused by lack of moisture; give it the protection provided by regular infusions of Dewyfresh, the drought-defying moisturizer.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> The Dewyfresh advertisement exhibits which one of the following errors of reasoning?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> (A) It treats something that is necessary for bringing about a state of affairs as something that is sufficient to bring about that state of affairs.\\r\\n> (B) It treats the fact that two things regularly occur together as proof that there is a single thing that is the cause of them both.\\r\\n> (C) It overlooks the fact that changing what people think is the case does not necessarily change what is the case.\\r\\n> (D) It relies on the ambiguity of the term “infusion,” which can designate either a process or the product of that process.\\r\\n> (E) It relies on an analogy between two things that are insufficiently alike in the respects in which they would have to be alike for the conclusion to be supported.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Argument Breakdown\\r\\n\\r\\n**Conclusion (thus)** Skin should get regular Dewyfresh moisturizer to protect it from damage caused by lack of moisture.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Evidence** Drought dries and cracks the earth, which the advertisement calls “the skin of the world.”\\r\\n\\r\\n**Evaluate** Given that dry ground cracks, how could skin still behave differently? Soil and human skin are different materials. The ad needs the two to resemble each other in the very process it is comparing. The phrase “skin of the world” is a metaphor, not evidence that a moisturizer affects skin the way rain affects soil. Even if skin needs moisture, nothing here establishes that Dewyfresh provides the promised protection.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Goal** Look for a criticism of an analogy between the earth and human skin that has not established the relevant similarity.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Choice Notes\\r\\n\\r\\n**(A) Wrong Flaw.** Necessary versus sufficient would require the ad to argue, for example, that because moisture is required for healthy skin, applying Dewyfresh guarantees beautiful skin. It does not make that formal move. Its evidence is the earth analogy.\\r\\n\\r\\n**(B) Wrong Flaw.** A common cause would explain why two observed events happen together. The ad does not report two correlated events and infer a shared cause. It compares two different things.\\r\\n\\r\\n**(C) Wrong Flaw.** The argument does not claim that changing beliefs changes physical reality. The opening addresses people who doubt moisturizers, but the evidence is about drought, not a change in what people believe.\\r\\n\\r\\n**(D) Wrong Flaw.** “Infusion” is used to mean an input of moisture in both places. The conclusion does not switch from a process to its product. The questionable switch is from ground to human skin.\\r\\n\\r\\n**(E) Correct.** Test the analogy\'s relevant feature. Dry soil cracks without water; does human skin respond to a moisturizer in the same way? The ad gives no reason to think so. Calling earth “skin” makes the analogy memorable but does not supply the biological similarity the conclusion needs.\\r\\n\\r\\n## 2. PT102-S2-Q18 · Flaw · Difficulty 3 · Answer E\\r\\n\\r\\n*Modelled on PT154-S2-Q12 (false choice), PT110-S2-Q11 (best versus only), and PT150-S2-Q4 (plans).*\\r\\n\\r\\n> President of Central Supply Company: Profits are at an all-time low this fiscal year because of decreased demand for our products. If this situation continues, the company may have to declare bankruptcy. So it is important to prevent any further decrease in profits. Consequently, the only options are to reduce planned expansion or to eliminate some less profitable existing operations.\\r\\n>\\r\\n> Which one of the following most accurately describes a flaw in the company president\'s reasoning?\\r\\n>\\r\\n> (A) It presumes without giving justification that survival of the company has been a good thing.\\r\\n> (B) It does not take into account that there are alternatives to declaring bankruptcy.\\r\\n> (C) It presumes without giving justification that only decreasing costs will prevent further profit losses.\\r\\n> (D) It does not allow for the possibility that profits will decrease only slightly during the next fiscal year.\\r\\n> (E) It does not take into account that there may be other ways to stop the decrease in profits.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Argument Breakdown\\r\\n\\r\\n**Conclusion (consequently)** The company\'s only options are to reduce planned expansion or eliminate some less profitable current operations.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Evidence** Demand and profit have fallen. Continued decline may cause bankruptcy, so preventing further profit decline matters.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Evaluate** Granted, the company needs to stop profits falling. Why must it choose one of those two cost cuts? It might increase revenue through a new product, revise prices, or find a third cost saving. The urgency of the goal does not prove an exhaustive list of ways to reach it. We need only one possible third way to challenge “only.”\\r\\n\\r\\n**Goal** Find the missing alternatives to stopping profit decline, not merely alternatives to bankruptcy.\\r\\n"}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"i":1,"status":"fulfilled","value":"---\\r\\ntype: draft\\r\\nsubject: LR Flaw batch 01, part B, 20 slots\\r\\nstatus: draft, not loaded\\r\\ncreated: 2026-09-28\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Flaw explanations: batch 01, part B\\r\\n\\r\\nBank wording and keys were checked against `projects/lsatu-wt-glossary/public/data/`; keys and text were also checked against the 2026-09-28 database pull. All 20 keys agree. Bank/database text differences in this set are typographic or encoding differences, not substantive wording differences. The `Modelled on` references are complete explanations in that database, selected for the reasoning pattern; the corpus neighbor scan was run for all 20 slots. All choice-note tags occur in the existing database vocabulary. No question bank or database edits are part of this draft.\\r\\n\\r\\n## PT109-S3-Q5 | Flaw | D\\r\\n\\r\\n**Modelled on:** PT150-S2-Q4 (comparison), PT141-S4-Q3 (exposure and baseline), PT139-S4-Q18 (quantity distinction).\\r\\n\\r\\n### Argument Breakdown\\r\\n\\r\\n**Conclusion:** Radiation absorbed by airline flight crews does negligible harm.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Evidence:** Radiation absorbed on *one ordinary commercial flight* is no more dangerous than radiation from *one ordinary dental X-ray*, and one dental X-ray does negligible harm.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Evaluate:** The comparison changes its unit. A passenger takes one flight; a crew member takes many. Even if one exposure is harmless, repeated exposures might add up to harmful levels. Ask the author to compare cumulative exposure over the same period, not one flight against one X-ray.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Goal:** Find the objection that dose depends on duration and frequency, which the one-flight comparison omits.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Choice Notes\\r\\n\\r\\n**(A) Out of Scope.** Other kinds of dangerous radiation do not challenge the conclusion about the radiation crews actually absorb. This would help only if crews were exposed to one of those other kinds.\\r\\n\\r\\n**(B) No Impact.** A dental X-ray might offset some other risk, but the evidence says the X-ray itself does negligible harm. The conclusion concerns radiation harm, not total health benefits of dentistry versus flying.\\r\\n\\r\\n**(C) Out of Scope.** Higher-intensity X-rays may be harmful. The argument compares an ordinary dental X-ray to an ordinary flight; it does not claim that every X-ray exposure is harmless.\\r\\n\\r\\n**(D) Correct.** The more often and longer someone is exposed, the more radiation that person can absorb. Crew members\' repeated flights could cause nonnegligible harm even if the radiation from a single flight is as harmless as that from a single dental X-ray. This is the missing difference in the comparison.\\r\\n\\r\\n**(E) Out of Scope.** Additional risks of flying may matter to airline crews\' overall health, but the conclusion is limited to harm from radiation. An objection needs to make the radiation conclusion doubtful.\\r\\n\\r\\n## PT110-S3-Q4 | Flaw | E\\r\\n\\r\\n**Modelled on:** PT147-S1-Q6 (unrepresentative sample), PT120-S3-Q8 (rate versus cause), PT109-S4-Q1 (sampling).\\r\\n\\r\\n### Argument Breakdown\\r\\n\\r\\n**Conclusion:** The overwhelming majority of high school students want to finish, so a high *national* dropout rate could not be due to students\' lack of desire.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Evidence:** More than 89 percent of 1,000 randomly selected students at three schools in one medium-sized city said they planned to finish.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Evaluate:** Random selection can make a sample representative of the population *from which it was drawn*. It does not make three schools in one city representative of the nation. Imagine that other regions have very different dropout pressures or aspirations. Also, a plan to finish is not proof that a student will finish, though the answer set focuses on the first gap.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Goal:** Look for an objection to projecting a local survey result to students nationwide.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Choice Notes\\r\\n\\r\\n**(A) Wrong Flaw.** Eighty-nine percent is plainly a large majority. Quibbling over the word \\"overwhelming\\" would not expose the national sampling problem.\\r\\n\\r\\n**(B) Bad Description.** Wanting to finish and dropping out can coexist. The two conclusions concern students\' desire and a possible explanation of a dropout rate, not logically conflicting outcomes.\\r\\n\\r\\n**(C) Not an Objection.** The argument says *if* the national dropout rate is high, lack of desire cannot explain it. It does not need a high rate actually to exist to make that conditional claim.\\r\\n\\r\\n**(D) Bad Description.** Students can want to finish and still leave school. The author does not contradict himself by discussing both possibilities.\\r\\n\\r\\n**(E) Correct.** The respondents are from three schools in one medium-sized city, while the conclusion covers high school students nationwide. Even a large, randomly selected sample can be unrepresentative when drawn from the wrong population.\\r\\n\\r\\n## PT111-S3-Q13 | Flaw | D\\r\\n\\r\\n**Modelled on:** PT148-S1-Q2 (rate and total), PT120-S4-Q23 (timeframe), PT151-S4-Q23 (track the conclusion\'s exact claim).\\r\\n\\r\\n### Argument Breakdown\\r\\n\\r\\n**Conclusion:** The Planning Board exaggerates when it estimates that businesses are leaving at about four a week.\\r\\n"}'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"i":2,"status":"fulfilled","value":""}'}]
